label: Chapter 6
title: Rebuilding while the world keeps publishing
dek: Phones, JavaScript and machine-readable data changed what the web expected. WordPress had to change too, without breaking the sites already standing on it.

blocks.text: Imagine renovating a building whose tenants cannot be asked to move out. By September 2013 one website in five ran on WordPress,[^w3-2013] with plugins and themes written to the habits of a decade. Whatever changed had to keep all of that working.

blocks: The contributors’ handbook makes it policy: “WordPress strives to never break backward compatibility.”[^version-numbering] The price was patience. For almost eight years WordPress supported the same old version of PHP, the language it is written in, because sites still ran on it.[^php-min]

So the renovation went room by room. In 2013 a group led by the designer Matt Miklic rebuilt the admin’s look as a plugin, MP6, releasing it weekly to anyone who would try it;[^mp6] that December it became the face of WordPress 3.8, which would “adapt” to phone, tablet or desk.[^wp38] Build it as a plugin, merge it when ready: this became the method.[^features-plugins] Weeks earlier, 3.7 had begun installing security fixes by itself — “Updates while you sleep.”[^wp37]

blocks.name: viewport
blocks.caption: One post, three destinations. The third is what a program receives when it asks the REST API for the same post: no design, only structured data. The field names are the real ones; the response is abridged.

blocks: One structural change took four years. Ryan McCue’s idea was that any program — a phone app, another site — should be able to read and write a WordPress site’s content as plain data, through what is called a REST API.

blocks.name: track
blocks.caption: A plan written in 2015 expected the content endpoints one release after the infrastructure. They took three.[^rest-2015]

steps.label: Experiment
steps.text: A proof of concept, made at a contributor summit.[^rest-2016]

steps.label: Feature plugin
steps.text: A Google Summer of Code project, then two versions of a plugin kept going by a small team.[^rest-2013][^rest-2015]

steps.label: Infrastructure in core
steps.text: WordPress 4.4 ships what McCue called an “API construction kit”, without the content itself.[^wp44][^rest-infra]

steps.label: Public endpoints
steps.text: WordPress 4.7: posts, comments, terms, users and more, on by default.[^wp47]

blocks: Even then, something went wrong. Six weeks after 4.7 a flaw was reported that let strangers rewrite posts. The fix went out silently through automatic updates; attackers still defaced pages on an estimated 40,000 sites that had not updated, by the security firm Wordfence’s count.[^rest-disclosure][^defacements]
Meanwhile Automattic had rebuilt WordPress.com’s interface in JavaScript, and in December 2015 Mullenweg set a conference audience some homework: “Learn JavaScript, deeply.”[^calypso][^js-deeply]

blocks.label: Meanwhile, the share
blocks.text: By W3Techs’ measure, WordPress ran 13.1% of all websites in early 2011 and 30% by March 2018.[^w3-2018]

blocks.title: The cost of never breaking things

items.text: It works for users now. When it stops working for them, it’s our fault and we lose their trust.
items.where: quoted by Aaron Jorbin in “User Trust Matters”, 2017

items.text: Two of the things that helped make WordPress the strong, stable, powerful tool it is — backward compatibility and working without JavaScript — were actually holding it back.

Mullenweg was writing about WordPress.com’s interface, not the core software; the tension he names was the same one. Version 3.2 (2011) dropped PHP 4; the minimum then stayed at PHP 5.2 until version 5.2 raised it in May 2019.[^php-min]
No partial endpoints in core. Let’s design a complete API, not half-do it and foist it on millions of sites.
items.where: project chat, as reported by WP Tavern

items.text: We’ve got a bit of a chicken and egg: without core adoption, potential API consumers are hesitant to take the plunge, but without adoption it won’t be tested sufficiently to be merged.
WP Tavern counted “just four major contributors operating at less than part time” on the project at that point.[^rest-gridlock]
The first official mobile app, WordPress for iPhone.[^iphone]
The theme customizer arrives in 3.4: change a design and watch a live preview.[^wp34]
Version 4.2 moves databases, where it can, to a fuller character set — which brings emoji.[^wp42]
Version 4.4 makes images responsive with no work from theme authors.[^wp44]
A rule is announced: all new or updated code must meet the WCAG 2.0 accessibility guidelines at level AA. “We’re not there yet,” the announcement adds.[^a11y-2016]
